title: When to hedge
objectives: Decide when to hedge a bet that is already running.

screens.title: Lock it in
screens.prose: You backed a team at 5 to 1 for £100: you win £500 or lose £100. Now you can bet on the other side at evens. Drag the hedge along the top line.

state.caption: Hedge £50: £450 if your team wins, −£50 if it loses

derive.caption: Hedge {{money(p1.x, "£", 0)}}: {{money(500 - p1.x, "£", 0)}} if your team wins, {{money(p1.x - 100, "£", 0)}} if it loses

screens.question: Drag to the hedge that pays the same whichever side wins.

hints.text: A hedge of $h$ costs $h$ if your team wins and pays $h$ if it loses.
You want $500 - h = h - 100$.
That is where the two lines cross: $h = 300$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the two lines cross.

byKey.p1: The two outcomes still differ. Move to where the lines cross.

explain.text: At $h = 300$ you make $500 - 300 = 200$ if your team wins and $-100 + 300 = 200$ if it loses. The hedge turns a bet into a certain £200. Two bets you can make copy the payoff you want.

screens.title: A better price
screens.prose: Same bet, but the other side is now offered at 2 to 1. A hedge of $h$ pays $2h$ if your team loses.

state.caption: The other side now pays 2 to 1: the bottom line is $2h - 100$.

screens.question: How much profit can you lock in?

hints.text: Find $h$ with $500 - h = 2h - 100$.
$h = 200$, so the profit is $500 - 200$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equate the two outcomes with the new price.

byKey.old: That is the evens answer. A better price on the hedge locks in more.

explain.text: Equating $500 - h$ with $2h - 100$ gives $h = 200$. Both outcomes then pay £300. A better hedge price costs less and locks in more.

screens.title: A series, one game at a time
screens.prose: You want £100 on a best-of-seven series: +£100 if your team wins it, −£100 if not. You can only bet game by game at evens. The leaves show what the series is worth after two games.

state.caption: Best of seven. Values after two games, worked back from the end.

screens.question: How much do you bet on game 1?

hints.text: At fair odds a node is worth the average of its two children.
After a win in game 1 you need +£31.25, the average of +£62.50 and £0. After a loss you need −£31.25.
Bet £31.25: a win takes £0 to +£31.25 and a loss to −£31.25.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the leaves to value each node after game 1.

byKey.whole: Betting £100 on game 1 is far more than the series bet. One game rarely decides a best-of-seven.
byKey.seventh: You spread £100 over seven games. The bets depend on the score.
byKey.half: That is the best-of-three bet. Seven games dilute game 1 more.

explain.text: Each node is worth the average of its children: ±£31.25 after game 1. Game 1 must move you from £0 to those values, so you bet £31.25. The formula $100 \times \binom63/2^6$ gives the same.

screens.title: One game each
screens.prose: The score is 1–1. Imagine games 4 to 7 played whatever happens. Game 3 matters only if it decides the series.

state.caption: Score 1–1 after a win and a loss.

screens.question: How much do you bet on game 3?

hints.text: Game 3 decides the series when the other four games split evenly.
Games 4 to 7 split 2–2 with chance $\binom42/2^4 = \tfrac{6}{16}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that game 3 decides the series.

byKey.same: That was the game 1 bet. At 1–1 the next game matters more.
byKey.half: That is the bet when two wins are needed by each side, at 2–2.

explain.text: If games 4 to 7 split 2–2, game 3 decides the series; otherwise it does not matter. That has chance $\tfrac{6}{16}$, so you bet $100 \times \tfrac{6}{16} = £37.50$. A closer score makes each game matter more.

screens.title: Always hedge?
screens.prose: You backed a team at 5 to 1 for £100, and you believe it now wins with chance 0.6. The other side is offered at evens. A friend says a locked profit is free money.
screens.question: What does a full £300 hedge cost you?

options.text: £60 of expected profit: £260 unhedged against £200 locked
Nothing: a hedge is free insurance
options.why: At these odds the hedge bets against your edge. It costs £60 of expected profit.

options.text: It adds expected profit by removing the risk
options.why: Removing risk does not add expectation. It swaps £260 of expected profit for a certain £200.

hints.text: Find the expected profit unhedged.
£260 unhedged against £200 locked.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the expected profit with the locked £200.

byKey.b: You called the hedge free. It bets on the side you think is the underdog, at evens.
byKey.c: A hedge cannot add expectation here. It trades £60 of it for certainty.

explain.text: Unhedged you expect $0.6 \times 500 - 0.4 \times 100 = £260$. The full hedge locks £200, giving back £60 of edge. Hedge only as far as your bankroll needs.

screens.title: How much to hedge
screens.prose: You hold that bet with a bankroll of £1,000 and believe $p = 0.6$. Use the log rule from l21 to size the hedge.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Unhedged, wealth ends at £1,500 with chance 0.6 or £900 with chance 0.4.
A hedge of $h$ at evens moves these to $1500 - h$ and $900 + h$.
Kelly picks $h$ to maximise $0.6\ln(1500 - h) + 0.4\ln(900 + h)$.
Set the derivative to zero: $\dfrac{0.6}{1500 - h} = \dfrac{0.4}{900 + h}$.
Hedge £300 to lock in £1,200, since a certain amount beats a gamble.
lines.why: A certain £1,200 has a lower expected log than the bet unhedged.

hints.text: Start from wealth in each outcome.
Then add the hedge, take expected logs and differentiate.
Outcomes, hedge, objective, derivative, solve, conclude.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the two unhedged outcomes.

byKey.d1: A sure £1,200 has log 7.090, below the unhedged 7.109. Hedging fully gives away edge.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the full hedge belongs.

explain.text: The expected log is 7.109 unhedged, 7.110 at $h = 60$ and 7.090 fully hedged. A small hedge trims the risk your bankroll cannot afford. The rest of the edge stays on.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Each hedge copied the payoff you wanted with bets you could make, working back from the end. At evens a node is worth the average of its children, and the bet is half their gap. Over a series, imagine every game played:

$$\text{bet} = \text{stake} \times P(\text{this game decides the series}).$$
screens.question: After a win your position is worth +£50, after a loss −£10. What do you bet on this game at evens?

hints.text: The bet is half the gap between the children.
Bet £30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve the gap between the two values.

byKey.gap: That is the whole gap. A win adds the bet and a loss takes it away, so the bet is half the gap.
byKey.avg: That is the node's value. The bet is half the gap.

explain.text: The node is worth $\tfrac12(50 - 10) = £20$. A £30 bet takes it to £50 on a win or −£10 on a loss. So the bet is half the gap, £30.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Four puzzles at about 3 minutes each; keep your own time and say each argument aloud. Evens on every hedge.
screens.question: Fill in the four answers, in pounds.

rows: You backed £50 at 3 to 1. Hedge to lock in?
The same bet. Profit locked in?
£100 on a best-of-three, game by game. Game 1 bet?
You won game 1 of that best-of-three. Game 2 bet?

hints.text: Equate the two outcomes; for the series, ask when a game decides it.
Hedge £100 to lock £50. Game 1 is decisive with chance $\tfrac12$, and so is game 2 at 1–0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r2c1: Game 1 decides a best-of-three when games 2 and 3 split: chance $\tfrac12$.
byKey.r3c1: At 1–0, game 2 matters only if game 3 would be lost: chance $\tfrac12$.

explain.text: The hedge of £100 locks in £50 either way. Game 1 of a best-of-three decides it with chance $\tfrac12$, so bet £50. At 1–0 a win ends it and a loss leaves a decider. The gap is £100, so the bet is £50.

screens.title: Follow-up: best of five
screens.prose: You found £31.25 for game 1 of a best-of-seven. The interviewer asks about a best-of-five, still £100 on the series.
screens.question: How much do you bet on game 1?

hints.text: Imagine games 2 to 5 played.
Game 1 decides the series when they split 2–2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that games 2 to 5 split 2–2.

byKey.seven: That is the best-of-seven bet. A shorter series makes game 1 matter more.
byKey.fifth: You spread £100 over five games. The bet depends on how often game 1 decides it.

explain.text: Games 2 to 5 split 2–2 with chance $\binom42/2^4 = \tfrac38$. So bet $100 \times \tfrac38 = £37.50$ on game 1. Shorter series put more on each game.

screens.title: Hedging an option
screens.prose: A share trades at £100 and will move to £110 or £90. A call option with strike £100 then pays £10 or £0. You sold the call and want to hedge it with shares.
screens.question: How many shares should you hold per call sold?

hints.text: Match the call's two payoffs with shares.
The call's payoff gap is £10; the share's gap is £20.
Hold $10/20 = 0.5$ shares.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gap in the call's payoff by the gap in the share price.

byKey.one: One share moves £20 between the outcomes, twice the call's £10 gap.
byKey.tenth: You divided £10 by £100. Use the gap between the share's two prices.

explain.text: The call's payoff changes by £10 when the share's price changes by £20, so hold 0.5 shares. That is the series bet again: the gap in what you owe over the gap in what you can trade. Redoing it at every step is delta hedging, as in trees l12.

ideas: To lock a profit, size the hedge so both outcomes pay the same.
At evens the bet is half the gap between the two next values: stake times the chance the game decides it.
A fair hedge cuts variance, not expectation; a worse one gives back edge. Hedge only what the bankroll needs.

formula.name: Series bet at evens
formula.note: $r$ and $s$ are the wins each side still needs; $S$ is the series stake.

summary.trap: Hedging every bet, or calling a hedge at bad odds free. It gives back the edge.

quiz.prose: You backed a team at 5 to 1 for £100, and its true chance is now $\tfrac12$. You hedge £300 at evens.
quiz.question: What happens to your expected profit?

options.text: It stays £200: the hedge cuts the spread, not the expectation
It rises, because the risk is gone
options.why: Removing risk does not add expectation. Unhedged you also expect $250 - 50 = £200$.

options.text: It falls, because hedges always cost edge
options.why: At fair odds the hedge has zero expected value, so it costs nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the expected profit unhedged.

explain.text: Unhedged: $\tfrac12 \times 500 - \tfrac12 \times 100 = £200$. Hedged: a certain £200. This is the edge case: a hedge at fair odds changes the variance, not the expectation.

quiz.prose: £100 on a best-of-seven, game by game at evens. The score is 3–3.
quiz.question: How much do you bet on game 7?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does game 7 decide the series?

byKey.half: That is the bet at 2–2. At 3–3 game 7 settles everything.

explain.text: At 3–3 game 7 decides the series for certain. So the game bet equals the whole series bet, £100.

quiz.prose: You backed £20 at 4 to 1. The other side is offered at evens.
quiz.question: How much profit can you lock in?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $80 - h = h - 20$.

byKey.hedge: That is the hedge. The locked profit is $80 - 50$.
byKey.eighty: That is the unhedged win. The hedge costs £50 of it.

explain.text: $80 - h = h - 20$ gives $h = 50$. Both outcomes then pay £30.
